title: LC Tanks and Tuned Stages
intro: The resonator at the heart of an LC oscillator, its losses, and how a tank behaves as an amplifier load (Razavi, Section 15.3.1).

blocks.text: An inductor $L_1$ in parallel with a capacitor $C_1$ resonates where their reactances cancel, and the impedance there is infinite:

Real inductors have series resistance $R_S$ from the metal of the spiral. The inductor quality factor is $Q = L_1\omega/R_S$, only about 5 to 10 for on-chip spirals. With $R_S$ the impedance stays finite at every frequency; its peak is near $1/\sqrt{L_1 C_1}$, shifted slightly by $R_S$:

Over a narrow band, $L_1$ in series with $R_S$ behaves like $L_P$ in parallel with $R_P$. Equating the two impedances at $s = j\omega$ gives $L_P = L_1(1 + 1/Q^2)$ and $R_S R_P = L_1 L_P \omega^2$. For $Q$ above about 3:

The same trick turns a capacitor with series resistance into a parallel RC, with $Q = 1/(C\omega R_S)$. The whole tank then becomes three parallel elements $L_P$, $C_P$, $R_P$, and the parallel form gives the useful identity $Q = R_P/(L_P\omega)$.

blocks.alt: Two plots against log frequency. Top: the magnitude of the tank impedance, small far from resonance and peaking sharply at R_P at the resonant frequency. Bottom: the phase of the impedance, near plus 90 degrees below resonance, crossing zero at resonance and approaching minus 90 degrees above it.
blocks.caption: A parallel tank is inductive below resonance (positive phase), a pure resistance $R_P$ at $\omega_1$, and capacitive above.

blocks.text: Use the tank as the drain load of a common-source stage. At resonance the gain is $-g_m R_P$; near DC it is tiny because the inductor shorts the drain to $V_{DD}$. Tying the drain back to its own gate does not oscillate: at resonance the loop phase is 180° (just the inversion), and the tank's own phase never reaches the extra 180° needed.

A useful property: the inductor cannot hold a DC drop, so the drain's average voltage stays near $V_{DD}$ and the output swings symmetrically above and below the supply. With a good tank the peak-to-peak swing can exceed $V_{DD}$.

Tank loss sets everything downstream: start-up needs $g_m$ large compared with $1/R_P$, the amplitude is roughly current times $R_P$, and phase noise improves with Q. On-chip, $R_P$ is limited mostly by the inductor's series resistance.

blocks.title: Inductor loss as a parallel resistor
blocks.text: A 2 nH spiral has $Q = 8$ at 5 GHz. Find its series resistance, the equivalent parallel resistance, and the capacitance that resonates with it at 5 GHz.

blocks.title: Tuned-stage gain
blocks.text: The tank of the previous problem loads a common-source transistor with $g_m = 10\text{ mS}$. What is the gain at 5 GHz, and roughly what is it at DC if the bias is unchanged?
solution: At resonance the load is $R_P$: $A_v = -g_m R_P = -10\text{ mS} \cdot 503\ \Omega \approx -5.0$.
At DC the load is just $R_S = 7.85\ \Omega$ (ignoring $r_o$), so $|A_v| \approx 0.08$: the stage cannot latch through its DC path.
blocks.answer: About −5 at resonance, below 0.1 at DC.

blocks.title: When the approximation fails
blocks.text: An inductor has $Q = 2$ at the frequency of interest. By what factor does the exact $L_P$ differ from $L_1$, and how does $R_P$ compare with $Q^2 R_S$?
solution: $L_P = L_1(1 + 1/Q^2) = 1.25 L_1$: a 25% error if you assume $L_P = L_1$.
Exactly, $R_P = L_1 L_P\omega^2/R_S = (1 + 1/Q^2)Q^2 R_S = 5 R_S$ rather than $4R_S$. The simple forms need $Q$ of about 3 or more.
